summary: Specifies the Inter-Chassis Communication Protocol, which lets provider edge devices in a redundancy group synchronize data to provide redundancy for VPWS and VPLS services. It supports both attachment circuit and pseudowire redundancy.

plainLanguage.summary: A provider that sells Layer 2 VPN services wants the service to survive the failure of one of its routers. The backup router has to know what the failed one was doing, so the two have to talk. This RFC defines that conversation: a protocol that runs inside the LDP session the two routers already have, in which they agree on the redundancy group they belong to, exchange the configuration of the services they protect, and tell each other when something changes.

how does iccp detect pe failure
subtitle: A protocol, carried inside LDP, that lets redundant provider edge routers share state so a backup can take over for a failed one.

tldr.problem: A carrier that offers Layer 2 VPN services needs a second router that can take over when the first one fails, and that backup has to know what the failed router was doing: which pseudowires were carrying traffic, which were on standby, and how the links into the customer were aggregated.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the Inter-Chassis Communication Protocol, which runs inside the LDP session between the provider edge routers, using new LDP message types. The routers form a redundancy group, exchange connection and application messages, and synchronize configuration and state so that both agree on what is active and what is standby.
tldr.outcome: Redundancy for pseudowires and for attachment circuits can span two routers instead of one, and the failure of one router is detected quickly enough for the other to take over within the service restoration time the customer contract requires.

today: RFC 7275 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2014, and the unit metadata lists no document that obsoletes or updates it. It registers the LDP message types 0x0700 to 0x0703, the ICCP capability TLV and the ICC RG parameter types, and it is the protocol that carries inter-chassis redundancy for L2VPN services.

sections.title: Why Two Routers Have to Talk
sections.content:
Network availability is a critical metric for service providers, because it bears directly on their profitability. Outages mean lost revenue and, for customers running mission-critical applications under tight service level agreements, contractual penalties. That is true of any carrier network, and networks using Layer 2 Virtual Private Network (L2VPN) technology are no exception. A high degree of availability can be achieved with intra-chassis and inter-chassis redundancy mechanisms, and this document concerns the latter.

The RFC defines an Inter-Chassis Communication Protocol (ICCP) that allows the synchronization of state and configuration data between a set of two or more provider edge nodes forming a Redundancy Group (RG). The protocol supports multi-chassis redundancy mechanisms on either the attachment circuits or the pseudowires. For the purposes of the document, a chassis is an L2VPN provider edge node.

The document assumes it is normal to run the Label Distribution Protocol (LDP) between the provider edges in the redundancy group, and that LDP components will in any case be present to establish and maintain pseudowires. ICCP is therefore built as a secondary protocol running within LDP, taking advantage of the LDP session mechanisms and of the underlying TCP transport and TCP-based security mechanisms already needed for LDP to operate.
sections.plainLanguage:
A carrier wants its Layer 2 VPN service to keep working when one of its routers dies, and to switch over fast enough to meet the availability it promises its customers. That needs a second router that can take over.

The backup cannot do that on its own. It has to know which pseudowires were carrying traffic, which were on standby, and how the customer connections were bundled, and it has to learn about changes as they happen. This RFC is the protocol for that exchange, and it rides inside the LDP session the two routers already run for pseudowires.

sections.title: The Redundancy Model and the Interconnect
sections.content:
The focus of the document is on provider edge node redundancy. The operator designates a set of two or more provider edge nodes to form a redundancy group. Members of a group fall under a single administration, and employ a common redundancy mechanism towards the access, that is the attachment circuits or access pseudowires, and towards the core, for any given service instance. Members may use disparate redundancy mechanisms for disjoint services. The devices may be offering any type of L2VPN service, VPWS or VPLS, and while the use of ICCP may even apply to Layer 3 service redundancy, that is outside the scope of the document.

The provider edges in a group offer multi-homed connectivity to individual devices, such as a customer edge or a DSLAM, or to entire networks such as an access network. Figure 1 of the RFC shows the model: a multi-homed customer node reaches two provider edges, PE1 and PE2, which are joined by an ICCP channel, and each of them holds pseudowires towards the core.

The redundancy mechanism towards the access node could be one of many technologies, for example IEEE 802.1AX link aggregation groups with LACP, or SONET Automatic Protection Switching; the specifics are outside the scope of the document. What is assumed is that the provider edges in the group must be able to communicate with each other for the access redundancy mechanism to work correctly, so an inter-chassis communication protocol must run among them to synchronize configuration and running state.

The presence of that channel also simplifies the pseudowire redundancy mechanism, because it lets the group run an arbitration algorithm to elect which pseudowires should be active and which standby for a given service instance. The result of the arbitration can then be advertised to the remote provider edges, instead of embedding a handshake procedure into the pseudowire redundancy status mechanism and into every other possible Layer 2 status mechanism.

The interconnect, meaning the links or networks over which ICCP messages travel rather than the customer traffic, has four possible arrangements. The provider edges may be physically co-located, in the same point of presence or central office, or geo-redundant, in different locations. The interconnect may be dedicated, with back-to-back links between the provider edges, or shared, running through the packet switched network such as the MPLS core. Co-located and shared interconnects can be protected by packet switched network mechanisms such as RSVP label switched paths with Fast Reroute or end-to-end backup paths, while co-located dedicated interconnects can use Layer 2 mechanisms such as link aggregation groups.
sections.plainLanguage:
The model is simple: two provider edge routers, both connected to the same customer network, and both holding pseudowires towards the core. The customer connects to both, so either can carry the traffic.

The two routers need a private channel between them for the control information. That channel can be a direct cable between two routers in the same building, or it can run across the provider's own core network to a router in another building.

Having that channel also simplifies the job. Instead of each router deciding independently which pseudowire should carry traffic, the two can run an election and tell the far end of the network the result.

sections.title: What the Protocol Has to Provide
sections.content:
The RFC sets out nine requirements for ICCP.

It MUST provide a control channel between the provider edges in a redundancy group, which may be co-located or remote. Client applications MUST use this channel only for control information and not for data traffic, so the protocol SHOULD provide relatively low bandwidth, low delay and highly reliable message transfer. It MUST accommodate multiple client applications, such as multi-chassis LACP, pseudowire redundancy and SONET APS, which means the messages SHOULD be extensible and TLV-based, and the protocol SHOULD provide a robust application registration and versioning scheme.

It MUST provide reliable message transport and in-order delivery between nodes in a group, with secure authentication built in. The redundancy applications that use ICCP expect reliable transfer and will assume the protocol deals with flow control and retransmissions. Because those applications rely on ICCP to synchronize state machines on separate nodes, in-order delivery is critical: lost messages or messages arriving out of sequence would harm the client applications.

It MUST provide a common mechanism to monitor the health of the provider edges in a group, used to detect a node failure or its isolation from the MPLS network in the shared interconnect case, and to inform the client applications. The applications require that the mechanism trigger failover according to the procedures of the redundancy protocol employed on the attachment circuit and pseudowire, and the solution SHOULD achieve sub-second detection of the loss of a remote node, around 50 to 150 milliseconds, to give the client applications enough reaction time to reach sub-second service restoration times.

It SHOULD provide asynchronous, event-driven state updates, independent of periodic messages, so that clients are told of a state change immediately, with application data sent on demand rather than on a timer. It MUST accommodate multi-link and multi-hop interconnects, including redundant paths between a pair of devices. It MUST ensure transport security between devices in a group, which matters most when the members are in different locations connected over a shared network: ICCP MUST NOT accept connections arbitrarily from any device, and some means of preventing source address spoofing MUST be in place.

Finally, it MUST allow the operator to configure the members of a group statically, with auto-discovery left for the future; it SHOULD allow flexible group membership, since two nodes will cover most deployments but the design must not preclude more, and a single node MUST be able to belong to several groups at once.
sections.plainLanguage:
The list of requirements is the real design brief for the protocol, and most of it is about what the applications on top of it can assume.

Three points stand out. The channel carries control information only, never customer traffic. Messages must arrive reliably and in order, because the applications use them to keep separate state machines in step, and a message arriving late or out of turn would corrupt them. And the loss of the far router must be noticed fast, in the region of 50 to 150 milliseconds, so that the failover can finish inside the restoration time the carrier promises.

sections.title: The Three Layers and the Transport
sections.content:
ICCP is modelled as three layers. The Application layer provides the interface to the redundancy applications that use ICCP. ICCP defines common connection management procedures and the message formats at this layer, but places no restrictions on the procedures or state machines of the clients, which are application specific and outside its scope. This guarantees implementation interoperability without placing unnecessary constraints on internal design.

The Inter-Chassis Communication layer implements the common services ICCP offers to the client applications: protocol versioning, redundancy group membership, redundant object identification, provider edge node identification, and ICCP connection management.

The Transport layer provides the actual message transport. It is responsible for addressing, route resolution, flow control, reliable and in-order message delivery, connectivity resiliency and redundancy, and finally provider edge node failure detection. The transport layer may differ depending on the physical layer of the interconnect.

On the membership side, when a provider edge is configured as a member of a group it first advertises the ICCP capability to its peers, then sends an RG Connect message to the peers that have also advertised the capability, and waits for them to send theirs. For a given group, the ICCP connection between two devices is operational only when both have sent and received RG Connect messages for that group. A device MUST reject an incoming RG Connect message if it is not a member of the group, or if the maximum number of simultaneous ICCP connections it can handle is exceeded; otherwise it MUST bring the connection up by answering with an RG Connect. A PE sends an RG Disconnect message to tear the connection down for a group, which is unilateral and needs no acknowledgement, and the connection for a group MUST be operational before any client application can use ICCP services in it.

Redundant objects, the things being protected, such as links, bundles and VLANs, are identified by a 64-bit opaque identifier called the Redundant Object ID (ROID). The ROID MUST match between group members for the protected object in question, which lets separate systems use a common handle for the protected entity whatever its nature, physical or virtual, and in a way that does not depend on how each system implements it.
sections.plainLanguage:
The protocol is built in three parts. The top part is where each redundancy application does its own work; the protocol only defines how those applications connect and what their messages look like. The middle part is the machinery common to all of them: which group a router belongs to, how versions are negotiated, and how a connection is set up. The bottom part is the transport, which handles the actual delivery of messages and detects when the far router has gone.

One idea is worth singling out. The thing being protected, a link, a bundle or a VLAN, is given a number that both routers use. It is an opaque handle: it means the same thing on both sides without either side having to describe the object in detail.

sections.title: The ICCP Connection State Machine
sections.content:
A provider edge keeps one ICCP connection state machine for every ICCP connection with a remote peer in the group. This machine is separate from the application connection state machine, and reacts only to RG Connect, RG Disconnect and RG Notification messages that carry no application TLVs. Actions and state transitions in the application connection state machines have no effect on it.

The machine has six states. NONEXISTENT is the starting point: no ICCP connection exists and there is no LDP session between the provider edges. INITIALIZED means an LDP session exists but the ICCP capability has not yet been exchanged. CAPSENT means the LDP session exists and the local provider edge has advertised its ICCP capability. CAPREC means it has both received and advertised the capability. CONNECTING means the local provider edge has initiated an ICCP connection and is awaiting a response. OPERATIONAL means the ICCP connection is operational.

The transition table is short. An established LDP session moves NONEXISTENT to INITIALIZED, and tearing the session down moves any state back to NONEXISTENT. Transmitting the ICCP capability moves INITIALIZED to CAPSENT, and receiving it moves INITIALIZED to CAPREC, with the action of transmitting the capability in return. Receiving the capability moves CAPSENT to CAPREC. Transmitting an RG Connect message moves CAPREC to CONNECTING. Receiving an acceptable RG Connect message moves CAPREC or CONNECTING to OPERATIONAL, with the action of transmitting an RG Connect in return, and receiving any other ICCP message moves CAPREC or CONNECTING back to CAPREC, with the action of transmitting a NAK TLV in an RG Notification message. Finally, receiving an acceptable RG Disconnect message, or transmitting one, moves OPERATIONAL back to CAPREC.
sections.plainLanguage:
Each connection between two routers runs through six states: no LDP session at all, then a session but no agreement to talk, then the capability advertised, then the capability exchanged in both directions, then a connection request sent, and finally the connection working.

Two transitions protect the connection. If a router in the CAPREC or CONNECTING state receives any ICCP message that is not an acceptable connection request, it drops back to CAPREC and answers with a rejection. And if the LDP session goes down at any point, the whole thing resets to the beginning.

sections.title: How the Messages Are Encoded
sections.content:
ICCP needs reliable, in-order, stateful message delivery and capability negotiation between provider edges, and LDP offers all of these and is already in wide use in the applications that would need the extensions. ICCP therefore takes advantage of the existing LDP infrastructure. Section 3.5 of RFC 5036 defines a generic LDP message structure, and a new set of LDP message types is defined to carry the ICCP information, using message types in the range 0x0700 to 0x070F.

Every ICCP message comprises an ICC-specific LDP header followed by message data. The header holds a U bit, which is the unknown message bit: on receipt of an unknown message, if U is clear a notification is returned to the originator, and if U is set the message is silently ignored. It holds the message type, which must be in the range 0x0700 to 0x070F, the message length in octets excluding the U bit, type and length fields, and a 4-octet message ID used by the sender to identify RG Notification messages that may apply to the message. The header then carries the ICC RG ID TLV, of type 0x0005 and length 4, holding a 4-octet unsigned integer that designates the redundancy group the sender belongs to; the value 0x00000000 is reserved. The rest of the header is the mandatory ICC parameters, which must appear in the order the individual message specifications give, and the optional ICC parameters, which may appear in any order.

An ICC parameter has a U bit and an F bit. The U bit is the unknown TLV bit: on receipt of an unknown TLV, if U is clear a notification MUST be returned to the originator and the entire message MUST be ignored, while if U is set the unknown TLV is silently ignored and the rest of the message processed as if it did not exist. The F bit applies only when U is set and the LDP message is to be forwarded: if F is clear the unknown TLV is not forwarded with the message, and if F is set it is. Setting both bits lets a TLV be propagated as opaque data through nodes that do not recognise it. The type is a 14-bit value and the length is the length of the TLV in octets, excluding the four header fields.

The Redundant Object Identifier is encoded as an 8-octet field holding an unsigned integer, with the value 0 reserved, and is carried inside application-specific TLVs.
sections.plainLanguage:
Because ICCP rides inside LDP, its messages are ordinary LDP messages with a new type number, in a range reserved for this purpose. Every one of them starts with a small header: the type, the length, an identifier the sender can use to refer to the message later, and the number of the redundancy group it belongs to. After that come the parameters, some required and in a fixed order, and some optional and in any order.

Each parameter carries two flags for the future. If a router does not recognise a parameter, it can either reject the whole message or ignore the parameter and carry on, and the flags say which. A second flag says whether an unrecognised parameter should be passed on when the message is forwarded.

sections.title: What the Client Applications Do
sections.content:
The RFC defines the procedures for two client applications: pseudowire redundancy (PW-RED) and multi-chassis LACP (mLACP). The PW-RED application SHOULD NOT be enabled together with an attachment circuit redundancy application for the same service instance, which simplifies the operation of the multi-chassis redundancy solution and removes the possibility of deadlock between the two mechanisms.

When a redundancy group is configured and multi-chassis pseudowire redundancy is enabled in it, the PW-RED application MUST send an RG Connect message with a PW-RED Connect TLV to each member of the same group. The sending router sets the A-bit to 1 if it has already received a PW-RED Connect TLV from its peer, and to 0 otherwise; a router that sent the TLV with the A-bit clear and then receives one from its peer MUST repeat its advertisement with the A-bit set. The PW-RED application connection is operational when both routers have sent and received PW-RED Connect TLVs with the A-bit set, and the two can then exchange RG Application Data messages. When the application is disabled or unconfigured for a group, the system MUST send an RG Disconnect message with a PW-RED Disconnect TLV.

Each router MUST advertise its local pseudowire configuration to the others in the group, so that they can build a view of the redundant nodes and pseudowires protecting the same service instances. The advertisement is initiated when the application connection first comes up, as an unsolicited synchronization carried in RG Application Data messages with PW-RED Config TLVs, delimited by a pair of PW-RED Synchronization Data TLVs. When the configuration changes, a router MUST re-advertise the most up-to-date information for the affected pseudowires.

The configuration advertisement carries the ROID of the pseudowire, which is used to correlate the pseudowires protecting each other on different routers, and the configured redundancy mode: Master Mode, Slave Mode, Independent Mode, or Independent Mode with Request Switchover. If the received redundancy mode does not match the locally configured mode for the same ROID, the router MUST respond with an RG Notification message rejecting the configuration TLV, MUST disable the associated local pseudowire until a satisfactory one arrives, and SHOULD raise an alarm. This guarantees that a misconfiguration does not lead to network-wide problems such as forwarding loops. A priority value is also advertised, used to determine which pseudowire takes the active role in a redundant setup, together with a service name that is global within the group and identifies which pseudowires belong to the same service, and the pseudowire identifier.

Status synchronization is done by sending the PW-RED State TLV whenever the pseudowire state changes on a router, at either the local or the remote end of the pseudowire, so that the group can work out per ROID which pseudowire will be used for forwarding and which will be on standby. A router may ask its peer to retransmit previously advertised state, which is useful when recovering from a soft failure, by sending one or more PW-RED Synchronization Request TLVs; the peer answers with the requested data in PW-RED TLVs delimited by a pair of PW-RED Synchronization Data TLVs.
sections.plainLanguage:
The client applications make the protocol useful. The pseudowire redundancy application has the two routers exchange the configuration of the pseudowires they each hold, so that both know which pairs protect the same service.

Each advertisement names the protected object, the redundancy mode, a priority that decides which of the pair takes the traffic, and the service the pair belongs to. If the two routers disagree about the mode for the same object, the one that receives the advertisement rejects it, stops using its own pseudowire until the disagreement is settled, and raises an alarm. Two routers both carrying the same service can send traffic in a loop.

State changes are pushed as they happen, and a router that has recovered can ask its peer to resend the state.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
ICCP SHOULD only be used in well-managed and highly monitored networks, and ought not be deployed on or over the public Internet. It is not intended to be applicable when the redundancy group spans provider edges in different administrative domains.

The security considerations of RFC 5036 and RFC 4447 that apply to the base LDP specification and to the pseudowire control protocol extensions apply to the capability mechanism described in the document. Implementations MUST provide a mechanism to select to which LDP peers the ICCP capability is advertised, and from which LDP peers ICCP messages are accepted, so an incoming ICCP connection request MUST NOT be accepted unless its source IP address is known to be the source of an eligible peer. The set of eligible peers could be preconfigured, as a list of IP addresses or address and mask combinations, or discovered dynamically through a secure discovery protocol. The TCP Authentication Option (RFC 5925) SHOULD be used, because it provides integrity and authentication for the ICCP messages and removes the possibility of source address spoofing; for backwards compatibility or ease of migration, the LDP MD5 authentication key option of Section 2.9 of RFC 5036 MAY be used instead. The security framework and considerations for MPLS in general, and LDP in particular, as described in RFC 5920 apply, as do the recommendations of RFC 6952 and the mechanisms aimed at addressing LDP's vulnerabilities.

Activity on the attachment circuits may cause security threats or be used to create denial of service attacks. A malicious customer edge implementation might trigger continuously varying LACP messages that lead to excessive ICCP exchanges, and excessive link bouncing of the attachment circuits would have the same effect; similar arguments apply to the inter-provider-edge MPLS links. Implementations SHOULD provide mechanisms to perform control-plane policing and mitigate these attacks.
sections.plainLanguage:
The protocol is meant for a network the operator controls. It should not be run over the public Internet, and it is not meant to join routers belonging to different operators, because the two ends exchange enough state about the customer's service that they must trust each other.

The protection comes from the LDP session underneath, and from an authentication option on the TCP connection. The important rule is that a connection is only accepted from an address the operator has said is eligible, so that a device that has merely found a way in cannot join the group.

One denial of service is called out: a customer device that keeps changing its link state could set off a storm of messages between the two routers, so control-plane policing is recommended.
